dedupe_keys.name: coastal storm flooding risk of the new york city subway under climate change gissr

description: This study estimates how coastal storms will flood the New York City subway as sea levels rise, and what that costs. Yuki Miura, Christine Blackshaw, Michelle Zhang, Kyle Mandli and George Deodatis extended the GIS-based Subdivision-Redistribution (GISSR) method, a fast physics-based flood estimator, to model flooding of subway tunnels and stations, and linked it to an input-output model of indirect economic losses from subway outage. The model was validated against observed subway flooding in Hurricane Sandy in 2012; each analysis of above- and below-ground flooding in Lower Manhattan runs in under 90 seconds on a single 4-core laptop processor. Scenario analyses, designed with New York City stakeholders, combine sea level rise projections with protective measures and are benchmarked against the city's ongoing resiliency projects; combining subway-specific and coastal measures proved most effective. Coverage: Lower Manhattan subway and surface, current and future storms. Access: article published in Transportation Research Part D in 2025; GISSR code on GitHub. Licence and cost: the article is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, free. Caveats: the economic input-output coefficients and the subway network representation are simplified, and results are specific to Lower Manhattan. It supports hazard exposure, cascading failure and climate adaptation planning for transit. It used the GISSR flood model catalogued here and relates to MTA open data and the Sandy network outage case study.
